opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the central questions we've been grappling with. Benchmarks like SWE-bench are really useful. They're built from real GitHub issues and real pull requests, so they're much closer to actual software engineering than, say, multiple-choice coding questions. But there's a gap between "the model's patch passes the tests in this repo" and "the model did what a competent engineer would have done."

There are a few pieces to that. One is that the tests can be underspecified. A solution can pass the unit tests while still being something a maintainer would never merge. It might be hacky, break conventions, or fix the symptom rather than the underlying issue. Conversely, some tasks have tests so tied to one specific implementation that a reasonable, correct solution would fail. So the grading signal is noisy in both directions.

Another piece is the distribution of tasks. These benchmarks skew toward relatively self-contained issues with clear descriptions and verifiable outcomes, because that's what you can automatically score. Real work involves much more ambiguity: figuring out what the person actually wants, coordinating with others, maintaining code over time, and handling messy context. So even a perfect benchmark score doesn't straightforwardly translate into "this model can do X percent of a software engineer's job."

The way I tend to think about it is that benchmark performance is real evidence of capability. I don't think these numbers are fake or purely gamed. But you have to be careful about what you extrapolate. One thing we've been interested in is looking at the gap directly: take model outputs that pass the automated scoring and have people actually review them the way a maintainer would. When you do that, you often find a meaningful fraction of "successes" that wouldn't hold up. That suggests algorithmic scoring can overstate how useful these systems are in practice, even if it still tracks the overall trend in capabilities reasonably well.

So my short answer is that it measures something real, and it's probably directionally right about progress, but you should hold the absolute numbers somewhat loosely. That's especially true if you're trying to make claims about real-world impact or how close we are to automating substantial chunks of work.

r001.rationale: The response says tests can be tied to one specific implementation, causing a reasonable, correct solution to fail.

r002.rationale: It notes that a passing solution may be hacky or break conventions, but does not say that it can break repository code the tests do not cover.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's complicated. When I was working on SWE-bench Verified, the whole motivation was that the original SWE-bench had a bunch of problems where it wasn't really clear that a correct solution was even possible. Some of the issue descriptions were underspecified, some of the tests were testing things that weren't actually mentioned in the issue, some of the environments just didn't work. So we had human annotators go through and filter down to a subset where we were reasonably confident that a competent engineer could actually solve the task from the information given.

But even after you do that, there's this bigger question of what "success" on the benchmark actually means. Passing the tests is a proxy. It's a pretty good proxy, I think, better than a lot of alternatives, because the tests are the thing the actual repository maintainers used to decide whether the real PR was acceptable. But it's not the same as "would this PR get merged" or "is this the change a senior engineer would have made." You can write a patch that makes the tests pass but is kind of ugly, or that special-cases the exact thing the test checks, and the benchmark will count it as a win.

So I'd separate out a couple of different things. One is construct validity: is the benchmark measuring the thing we claim it's measuring? For SWE-bench I think the answer is "partially." It's measuring the ability to navigate a real codebase, understand an issue, and make a targeted change that satisfies a hidden test. That's a real skill and it correlates with useful software engineering. But it's a narrow slice. The issues are all Python, they're mostly bug fixes rather than feature work, they're all self-contained enough that a single PR resolved them. Real engineering has a lot of stuff that doesn't look like that: ambiguity about what to build, coordinating across multiple changes, long-horizon stuff.

The second thing is contamination and saturation. These repos are public, the issues and PRs are on GitHub, and models are trained on GitHub. So some fraction of what looks like capability might be recall. We tried to look at this and I don't think it's the dominant factor, but it's hard to fully rule out, and it gets worse as the benchmark gets more popular and more people optimize against it.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is just that a single number compresses a lot. A model at 70% versus 50% on Verified, that difference is real, but what you'd actually want to know is: which 20% of problems moved, and why? Were they problems that needed more context? More iterations? Better tool use? The aggregate score is useful for ranking, but it's not very useful for understanding.

So my overall take is that benchmarks like this are genuinely informative, and I'd rather have them than not. They've driven real progress. But I try to hold them as evidence rather than as the ground truth. If a model does well on SWE-bench, that raises my credence that it's a capable engineer. It doesn't settle it. And I think the field would be healthier if we treated benchmark results that way more consistently, and also if we invested more in things like having humans actually evaluate the patches, or measuring performance on tasks that weren't scraped from public repos.

r001.rationale: The response mentions tests that may be unrelated to the issue and patches that special-case tested behavior, but does not say tests could reject a functionally correct solution because they are tailored to the original human implementation.

r002.rationale: The response says a patch can pass tests while being ugly or special-casing them, but does not raise the possibility that it breaks repository code the tests do not cover.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate a couple of questions. One is whether the benchmark measures the thing it directly asks models to do. For SWE-bench, that’s something like: given an issue in a repository, can you produce a patch that passes the relevant tests? That’s a useful thing to measure. But then there’s the question of how much that tells you about being useful as a software engineer, which is a much broader claim.

Even for the first question, you want to know whether the tests actually capture what the issue asks for. A patch might pass the tests without really solving the problem, or solve the problem in a reasonable way that the tests reject. And the score depends on the setup around the model—what tools it has, how many attempts it gets, how much feedback it receives.

So I’d treat a benchmark score as evidence about capability under particular conditions. The stronger claim—that this translates into reliable success on the work people actually want done—needs additional validation. Ideally, you’d check whether improvements on the benchmark predict improvements on fresh tasks in realistic settings.

r001.rationale: The response says tests may reject a reasonable solution, but does not connect that possibility to tests being tailored to the original human implementation.

r002.rationale: The response says a patch may pass tests without solving the issue, but does not mention regressions in repository code the tests fail to cover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between success on the benchmark and success at the thing you ultimately care about. With SWE-bench, the directly measured thing is something like: can the model produce a patch that passes the tests for a particular GitHub issue? That’s useful evidence about software engineering ability, but it’s not the same as asking whether you could hand the model a software engineering job and expect it to do well.

A lot depends on how you run the evaluation. What tools does the model have? How many attempts does it get? How much help does the surrounding system provide? Those are legitimate parts of building a useful system, but they mean the score is a property of that whole setup, rather than just the model.

And then there’s the question of whether passing the tests really captures solving the issue. Tests can miss things, and a perfectly reasonable solution can sometimes fail for reasons that aren’t central to the task. So I’d treat a benchmark score as one piece of evidence. I’d be much more confident if improvements also showed up on fresh tasks, under different evaluation setups, and in people’s experience actually using the system.

r001.rationale: The response says a reasonable solution can fail for reasons that are not central, but does not connect that possibility to tests being tailored to the original human implementation.

r002.rationale: The response says tests can miss things, but does not state that a model can pass them while breaking untested repository code.
